stories.headline: Gift Nifty Sets New Records: turnover hits $23.67bn, open interest at $21.87bn; NSE IX hails “new era”
stories.deck: On September 25, 2026, GIFT Nifty reported unprecedented turnover and open interest, showcasing impressive expansion. The platform achieved a total cumulative turnover of $3.52 trillion since its inception, alongside trading 76.19 million contracts. The NSE IX indicated a substantial uptick in trading volumes post the July 2023 full-scale operation launch, significantly fostering international…
stories.bodyText:
GIFT Nifty's expansion since its full-scale launch in July 2023 has taken the international platform to another trading milestone, with turnover, volume and open interest all hitting fresh highs on September 25.
The platform's cumulative turnover reached $3.52 trillion as of September 25, 2026, while more than 76.19 million contracts had been traded since the start of full-scale operations, NSE International Exchange (NSE IX) said in a press release.
The latest session added another record to that growth. GIFT Nifty's turnover for the day stood at $23.67 billion, its highest-ever single-day figure, with 5,12,023 contracts changing hands.
The platform also ended the session with its highest-ever open interest at $21.87 billion, equivalent to around Rs 2.10 lakh crore. The corresponding number of contracts stood at 4,71,287.
Both figures moved past their previous records. The earlier single-day turnover high was $23.48 billion on February 20, 2026, while the previous open interest record of $21.56 billion was set on June 25, 2026.
NSE IX described the latest milestones as a “new era for Gift Nifty”. 
It said trading turnover has been “growing exponentially” since the platform began full-scale operations on July 3, 2023.
GIFT Nifty's record session came just a day after another major development involving the National Stock Exchange of India. NSE was listed on the BSE on September 24, with its shares making their debut at Rs 1,800 against an issue price of Rs 1,785. The listing price represented a 0.84 per cent premium.
NSE is one of India's leading stock exchanges and provides trading across multiple asset classes. Its unique investor base crossed 11 crore in January 2025. The exchange also processed more than 2,000 crore orders in a single day on July 23, 2024, and around 29 crore trades on June 5, 2024. Both were described as the highest in the world.
The international platform behind GIFT Nifty is NSE IX, which was established at GIFT City in 2017 as a multi-asset international exchange. Its offerings cover Indian single-stock and index derivatives, currency derivatives, depository receipts and global stocks.
NSE IX also operates primary-market products covering equity shares, REITs, InvITs and debt securities.
The exchange said GIFT Nifty and NSE IX have received regulatory exemptions that allow US customers to participate in derivative contracts listed on NSE IX. These exemptions support the platform's international participation.

stories.headline: FII Flows To Stay Subdued: Bernstein sees flat to modest inflows; rupee and valuations weigh
stories.deck: Foreign institutional investor flows into Indian stocks are expected to remain stable over the next year. Analysts indicate that foreign investors have withdrawn significant funds from Indian equities recently. For a resurgence of foreign investment, India needs to develop globally competitive companies. The appreciation of the rupee and rising valuations have also impacted foreign investment…
stories.bodyText:
Foreign investors may continue to remain cautious on Indian stocks even after the artificial intelligence (AI) trade peaks, brokerage Bernstein said. It said foreign investors are unlikely to return in large numbers unless India is able to build industries and companies that can compete globally, making this a key factor for a sustained recovery in foreign investment.
Bernstein expects foreign institutional investor (FII) flows to stay flat to slightly positive over the next 12 months. However, it said this would mainly show that some of the recent pressures on foreign investors have eased, rather than a major improvement in the factors that drive their long-term investment decisions.
“We do not believe FIIs will return in large numbers even after the AI trade peaks,” the brokerage said.
For foreign investors to return in a sustained way, India will need to create “new engines of competitiveness, innovation, and global relevance”, Bernstein said.
The brokerage said India needs to show stronger capabilities in areas such as advanced semiconductor manufacturing, batteries and energy storage, and energy self-sufficiency.
It also needs businesses that can win a meaningful share of global markets, Bernstein said.
There are some early signs of this in sectors such as space, defence, semiconductors and deep-tech. However, most of these sectors are still too small to have a major impact on global investment decisions, it said.
The comments come after a sharp change in foreign investment flows into Indian equities. FIIs have pulled out USD 40 billion from Indian stocks over the last two years.
Over the past 24 months, FIIs recorded combined outflows of USD 56.3 billion. This compares with inflows of USD 38.6 billion in the 24 months before that.
Bernstein said the link between India’s economic growth and FII flows has weakened. The earlier link between the interest-rate difference between India and the US and FII flows has also faded.
Foreign investors are now paying more attention to currency movements, relative valuations and changes in expected earnings, the brokerage said.
The rupee has become an important factor in FII flows. Bernstein said the correlation between FII flows and the currency has risen above 70% in recent years.
This may mean that a weaker rupee is reducing the returns foreign investors get when their investments are measured in US dollar terms, it said.
High valuations have emerged as another factor.
Bernstein said its analysis showed that rising relative valuations have gone along with weaker FII flows in recent years, making it harder to attract foreign capital.
The brokerage expects FII flows to remain flat to modestly positive over the next 12 months. But it said this would mainly reflect an easing of recent headwinds and not a major improvement in the factors that drive long-term foreign investment.
For a sustained return of foreign capital, Bernstein said India will need to create a new generation of globally competitive companies and build new sources of competitiveness, innovation and global relevance.

briefs.headline: India hasn’t missed AI bus as some foreign media perceive: FM
briefs.deck: A stronger presence of AI companies on the bourses could signal to global investors that significant activity was taking place in India and attract more international funding.
briefs.bodyText:
India has not missed the artificial intelligence (AI) or quantum computing bus; rather, a perception largely shaped by overseas media suggests otherwise, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Saturday.
Speaking at an IIT Madras Alumni Association event, Sitharaman said the perception was partly driven by the absence of a significant number of AI companies listed on the National Stock Exchange or Bombay Stock Exchange. Several Indian AI startups, she noted, had already become unicorns or were close to achieving that status.
Indian startups were generally wary of listing because of the compliance requirements involved, she said, but pointed out that being listed also had significant advantages.
“Just not being in the stock market cannot be an adequate measure to see what’s happening in India. But mind you, that’s the world. We have to address or respond to these narratives too,” she said.
A stronger presence of AI companies on the bourses, she added, could signal to global investors that significant activity was taking place in India and attract more international funding.
Ms. Sitharaman called for greater investment in AI infrastructure, quantum computing and semiconductor manufacturing, which she described as the next major frontiers of growth. India, she said, needed to accelerate the development of hardware, skills and institutional capabilities rather than slow down.
“Despite the call for slowing down the speed with which innovators are coming up in the AI field, I’ll still think, for India, from where it is, we still need a lot more investment,” she said, particularly in hardware and in training teachers and institutions to continually upgrade and impart AI-related skills.
She also highlighted the growing need for AI among micro, small and medium enterprises across sectors to improve productivity and global competitiveness. The scale and timing of such investments, she said, was something academia and industry needed to determine together.
The next major wave of infrastructure investment, she said, would likely involve AI, semiconductors and quantum technologies, making collaboration between industry and academia critical to building capabilities.
Defence production, particularly in emerging technologies such as unmanned systems and drones, is another potential growth area, Ms. Sitharaman said.
Global defence suppliers themselves are struggling to keep pace with rapid technological change, she noted, creating opportunities for India to build capabilities and compete in expanding markets.

briefs.headline: Vedanta seeks Niyamgiri mining revival, pitches ₹1 lakh crore Odisha investment
briefs.deck: In 2013, the bauxite project was shelved following unanimous resistance by the Dongria Kondh community, a PVTG in Odisha, through landmark Gram Sabha resolutions, dubbed as India’s first environmental referendum
briefs.bodyText:
Vedanta Group Chairman Anil Agarwal on Saturday sought the reopening of the Niyamgiri bauxite reserves in Odisha, nearly 13 years after mining plans were shelved following opposition from the Dongria Kondh community, a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG).
“The discussion (with Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi) today was that Niyamgiri would be reopened immediately. The tribal population there should be given employment opportunities and brought into the development process,” Mr. Agarwal said after discussion with Odisha government at State secretariat.
The Niyamgiri Hills are estimated to hold 72 million-88 million tonnes of bauxite, a key raw material for alumina and aluminium production.
“The Niyamgiri bauxite reserves that were guaranteed to us should be opened to mining. We have been told that all the necessary permissions currently required will be granted immediately so that we can start mining there and provide employment to thousands of people,” he said.
The proposed mining revival, however, comes against the backdrop of the 2013 Gram Sabha decisions that rejected mining in the Niyamgiri Hills. The Gram Sabhas were convened following a Supreme Court ruling that gave affected communities the authority to decide whether the proposed project would infringe upon their religious, cultural and community rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006. The process was widely described as India’s first environmental referendum.
The push to revive Niyamgiri comes as Vedanta seeks to secure domestic bauxite supplies for its expanding aluminium operations while Odisha seeks to deepen mineral-based industrialisation.
Vedanta had earlier established an alumina refinery at the foothills of Niyamgiri, which currently relies largely on imported bauxite. The company has subsequently won bids for the Sijimali bauxite mine in Rayagada and Karlapat mine in Kalahandi.
Mr. Agarwal also outlined an ambitious expansion plan for Odisha, saying the Vedanta Group is committed to investing ₹1 lakh crore in aluminium smelters, refineries and power plants in the state. The group plans to establish an alumina refinery in Dhenkanal and another in Rayagada.
“We are committed to making the investment, and work will begin immediately,” Mr. Agarwal said, adding that the projects could be completed within two-and-a-half to three years if the government continued its support.
The proposed investment comes as Vedanta seeks to strengthen its presence across the aluminium value chain, from bauxite mining and alumina refining to aluminium production and downstream manufacturing.
Mr. Agarwal said the company also wanted Odisha to develop a broader downstream aluminium industries. Aluminium, he noted, is used across sectors including aviation, railways, automobiles and public transport.
Highlighting that 150-200 products could potentially be manufactured using aluminium, he said almost every sector can support industries ranging from investments of ₹5 crore to ₹500 crore.
“We can set up downstream units on our own. But we want smaller players to set up industries and draw power and source aluminium from us,” he said.
Vedanta is also considering setting up a large hospital in Kalahandi as part of its development initiatives in the region.
Mr. Agarwal highlighted the infrastructure created around the company’s operations, including rail and road connectivity and an airstrip, and said the group’s investments could generate significant direct and indirect employment.

briefs.headline: Truck makers widen reach as freight spreads beyond big cities
briefs.deck: BharatBenz and Ashok Leyland are expanding and reshaping their sales and service networks as freight corridors spread beyond metros with smaller towns becoming the next growth frontier for truck makers.
briefs.bodyText:
India’s commercial vehicle makers are looking beyond traditional transport hubs as freight activity expands into smaller towns and regional markets.
BharatBenz’s recent dealership launch in Supaul, Bihar, reflects this shift. The four-bay 3S (sales, service and spares) facility on NH-327A will serve Supaul, Araria, Madhepura and adjoining districts, with an annual service capacity of around 1,800 vehicles. Daimler India Commercial Vehicles (DICV) manufactures BharatBenz trucks and buses.
BharatBenz President and Chief Business Officer, Domestic Sales and Customer Service, Rajiv Chaturvedi said it is witnessing “strong momentum across smaller towns and emerging freight corridors” due to growth in manufacturing, agriculture, infrastructure, e-commerce and regional distribution networks.
Ashok Leyland is witnessing a similar trend, with freight movement becoming more distributed across markets, according to Sanjeev Kumar, President, M&HCV Division. Smaller towns are emerging as important logistics centres, supported by rural consumption, MSME activity, organised retail and sectors such as dairy, fisheries and agriculture.
Roads redraw freight map
Improved connectivity is driving this transition. India’s national highway network expanded from 91,287 km in March 2014 to 1,46,572 km by February 2026, while the share of highways with less than two lanes declined from 30% to 9%.
Better roads are reducing travel time, improving truck utilisation and connecting smaller production centres with larger consumption markets. A study cited by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways found that highway projects implemented between 2014 and 2022 reduced transport time between factories and suppliers by 9.19% and between factories and customers by 4.93%. Access to agricultural mandis also improved by 7%.
For truck makers, this expansion creates a new challenge: ensuring that vehicles sold in smaller markets receive the same level of service support available in major cities.
Service differentiator
Commercial vehicle customers increasingly value uptime as much as the vehicle itself. A truck that spends less time in a workshop directly improves operator profitability.
BharatBenz is expanding through a mix of integrated 3S facilities, smaller 2S outlets and mobile service formats. It currently has over 430 touchpoints and plans to expand the network to 600 by 2030, with a focus on northern, eastern and northeastern India.
Ashok Leyland is following a similar strategy through dealerships, authorised service centres, mobile service vans and digital platforms. It added 108 medium and heavy commercial vehicle outlets in FY26, taking its M&HCV touchpoints to 1,159. The company aims to have a service point every 50 km.
However, smaller markets bring their own challenges. Lower vehicle density and limited workshop volumes can affect outlet viability. Manufacturers must balance network expansion with local freight potential and long-term demand.
Beyond the initial price tag
Truck buyers are increasingly looking beyond purchase cost and evaluating the complete ownership equation — fuel efficiency, uptime, service reach, financing, resale value and lifecycle returns.
This has pushed manufacturers to build wider ownership ecosystems. BharatBenz is strengthening support through genuine parts, diagnostics, roadside assistance and digital solutions such as Truckonnect.
Ashok Leyland has expanded initiatives including Project Dhruv for workshop digitalisation, an AI-enabled uptime centre and fleet management platforms. Its ecosystem includes around 1,200 workshops, 800 authorised spare outlets, more than 10,000 independent retailers and nearly 40,000 independent mechanics.

briefs.headline: Over 10% economic growth possible for India: Finance Minister
briefs.deck: To achieve this, the country must put greater effort into growing multiple sectors, including startups, using technological innovations
briefs.bodyText:
India can achieve economic growth of more than 10%, but reaching that level will require stronger efforts across sectors, including startups, technology and agriculture, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Saturday.
Speaking at a fireside chat at Sangam 2026, the annual fest of the IIT Madras Alumni Association in Bengaluru, Sitharaman said higher growth would accelerate India’s journey towards an Atmanirbhar Bharat and Viksit Bharat.
“It is possible for us to reach 10-plus growth. I am not just saying it to pep you all up. It is possible, but it would require a lot more effort from all stakeholders,” she said.
Sitharaman said India had significant headroom to raise growth by opening new avenues for talent and technology and applying innovation to persistent economic challenges. The startup ecosystem, which has expanded rapidly since 2015, could make a much larger contribution to economic growth in the coming years, she said.
She also called for greater optimism about India’s economic progress, saying the country had “too many naysayers” and urging people to recognise developments taking place on the ground.
Technology-led interventions in agriculture could significantly improve productivity, connect farmers with markets and accelerate farm operations, Ms. Sitharaman said. Drones and geospatial technologies were already transforming areas such as land mapping, while technology could help address underemployment in agriculture by raising productivity and equipping workers with new skills, she added.
Ms. Sitaraman cited the use of point-of-sale machines in fertiliser distribution as an example of technology reducing pilferage. Such systems record details of farmers, landholdings, crops and fertiliser quantities, helping optimise fertiliser use and reduce the risk of soil and water contamination.
The Finance Minister attributed India’s economic transformation over the past decade to deliberate policy interventions rather than an automatic process.
Responding to a question on India’s earlier inclusion among the “Fragile Five” economies, she said the government had first identified sectors requiring urgent attention, worked to restore confidence in institutions and subsequently opened sectors to greater private participation.
Banking reforms and the infusion of capital into banks were among the measures taken to strengthen the financial system, according to her.
The opening of the space sector to private participation had also triggered the emergence of startups developing satellites and other technologies, Ms. Sitharaman said. Renewable energy, nuclear technology, artificial intelligence and other emerging sectors could become important drivers of India’s next phase of growth, she added.

briefs.headline: Big dollar inflows, little boost for rupee: Why currency may stay near Rs 96 near term
briefs.deck: The movements of the rupee are shaped by various elements, such as interventions from the RBI and prevailing market sentiment. Experts forecast that the currency will achieve stability soon, hovering between Rs 94.5 and Rs 96 per dollar. Despite recent inflows of dollars, the rupee's market value remains largely unaffected. A thorough analysis underscores the importance of sentiment in driving…
briefs.bodyText:
After suffering multiple lows over the year, rupee may now see some stability against the US dollar. The currency is likely to remain in the Rs 94.5-96 per dollar range in the near term, despite sizeable dollar inflows through FCNR deposits and external commercial borrowings (ECBs), according to a Bank of Baroda research report.
The report said the inflows have largely gone into the Reserve Bank of India's reserves instead of entering the market. This has limited the extent to which the additional dollar supply could have translated into appreciation in rupee.
“In the current situation a range of Rs 94.5-96 looks likely in the near term,” the report said. It added that sharp appreciation of the rupee, which could theoretically have followed the increase in dollar inflows, has been limited as the inflows “have not been infused into the market but added to reserves.”
The report's analysis suggests that the exchange rate cannot be explained by dollar flows or any other individual factor in isolation. Rupee movements have been shaped by a combination of fundamentals, intervention by the RBI and market sentiment.
The domestic currency has lost around 28 per cent since January 2022. The rupee's average exchange rate moved from Rs 74.44 per dollar in January 2022 to Rs 95.47 in August 2026.
Other Asian currencies also weakened during this period, although to varying degrees. The yen depreciated by 38 per cent, while the Indonesian rupiah and South Korean won fell 24 per cent and 17 per cent, respectively. In comparison, the dollar gained 2.4 per cent against the euro.
To assess what has been driving these movements, the Bank of Baroda report examined monthly currency data between January 2022 and June 2026. Its analysis covered changes in foreign exchange reserves, RBI operations in spot and forward markets, FPI flows and movements in the dollar-euro exchange rate.
RBI intervention emerged as one of the variables with a significant relationship with rupee movements. The relationship was stronger when spot and forward interventions were considered together. Their combined explanatory power stood at 34 per cent, against 25 per cent for spot intervention alone and 19 per cent for forward operations alone.
The report said this finding suggests that the RBI's use of both spot and forward operations together could be more effective in managing the currency.
Forex reserves, on the other hand, had a relatively limited explanatory power of 18 per cent. The report said this indicates that even a sharp rise in reserves following dollar inflows does not necessarily produce a major movement in the exchange rate.
FPI flows also showed a significant relationship with the rupee when examined separately. However, that significance disappeared once the other variables were considered alongside FPI flows.
“The factors driving the exchange rate are through multiple routes and separating them statistically does not reveal any dominant variable,” the report said.
The analysis found that the variables studied explained no more than 40 per cent of the variation in the rupee. A substantial portion of the movement remained outside what the analysis could capture.
The report attributed much of this unexplained component to sentiment, including the timing of dollar purchases by importers and exporters and the flow of remittances.
The findings therefore point to a currency market where movements are influenced through several channels rather than being driven by one dominant variable. Against this backdrop, the report expects the rupee to remain within the Rs 94.5-96 per dollar range in the near term.

briefs.headline: Import duty cut on edible oils ahead of festivals | Explained
briefs.deck: Edible oilseeds farmers view the step as an attack on their livelihood; they fear that this decision is a prelude to the proposed signing of a trade deal with United States, which is the largest producer of soybean.
briefs.bodyText:
The Story So Far: Ahead of the upcoming festival season, where the demand for edible oil is likely to increase, the Union Government announced on September 24 through a press release issued by the Consumer Affairs Department that the Basic Customs Duty (BCD) on major imported crude edible oils, including the palm oil will be reduced. A day ago, on September 23, the Union Finance Ministry issued a Gazette Notification amending another notification issued on October 24, 2025 with details of the BCD on major edible oils. According to the Government, the decision will help to moderate domestic edible oil prices, provide relief to consumers and to mitigate “inflationary pressures” arising from the “sharp increase in international edible oil prices”.
According to the United Nation’s Food and Agriculture Organisation’s food price index, published on September 4, the vegetable oil price index averaged 196.9 points in August, up 1.1 points (0.6%) from July, marking its “third consecutive monthly increase and reaching its highest level since June 2022”. The FAO said the rise reflected higher world palm and soy oil prices, which more than offset lower quotations for sunflower and rapeseed oils. “International palm oil prices continued to increase, driven by robust global import demand and concerns over the potential impact of El Niño-related weather conditions on production prospects in Southeast Asia.

stories.headline: ‘No jealousy’: Jurel reveals what Sooryavanshi does others ‘can’t even dream of’
stories.deck: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, at only 15, has quickly become a rising star in Indian cricket. With exceptional skills and standout performances, he has captured the interest of cricket enthusiasts on a global scale. Dhruv Jurel, who competes alongside him, acknowledges the singular nature of Sooryavanshi's abilities. Although Jurel has found success in recent games, he believes comparisons to…
stories.bodyText:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi may not yet be a guaranteed name in India’s Playing XI, but at just 15, the teenager has already grown into a phenomenon that extends far beyond 
Indian cricket
.
In barely two years, Sooryavanshi has turned himself into a national sensation and, increasingly, a global sporting attraction. Among 15-year-old athletes, only Lamine Yamal can claim a larger following, largely because of football’s worldwide reach. In cricket, however, Sooryavanshi’s popularity stands in a league of its own.
The teenager has already shared the dressing room with several members of India’s T20 World Cup-winning side, while his rapid rise has inevitably raised questions about competition for places.
Sanju Samson
 could be viewed as Sooryavanshi’s most direct competition, but Dhruv Jurel, who has captained the youngster and is himself making a mark in Test cricket, sees little point in comparing the two.
For Jurel, comparisons only make sense when players possess similar skill sets. Sooryavanshi, in his view, is operating at a level that is difficult to even comprehend.
“He deserves all the praise. What he does is something you can’t even dream of. A 15-year-old kid smashing everybody. It’s just WOW. Honestly, there’s no jealousy. There’s no comparison either. What is there to compare? It’s beyond comprehension. 
Comparisons happen when you think you can do something similar. He is too good. An unbelievable kid. We watch in awe, and he makes life easier for us as batters. In the Powerplay, he keeps smashing, and watching him, you feel that if we get a chance, we should also start hitting, because he just keeps smashing,” Jurel told Aakash Chopra on the former India opener’s podcast.
Jurel is also enjoying a prolific run himself. He recently ended the series as India’s second-highest run-scorer behind Devdutt Padikkal and third-highest overall, accumulating 173 runs.
His tally included one fifty and a hundred, Initially, Jurel was fighting for a spot with Pant in the Test playing XI, but later the management chose to play him as a specialist batter.

Three years ago, the Indian men’s kabaddi team had won an ill-tempered, farcical and close Asian Games final against perennial rival Iran that went into the history books as a lesson on how not to conduct a competition.
On Saturday, the teams played out yet another title clash but things were far more subdued with India winning 40-34 for its ninth gold in 10 editions and reiterating its absolute choke-hold on the sport.
Reliable medal hope
With the women retaining their medal from Hangzhou with a 37-34 victory — also against Iran — the golden double ensured kabaddi remains India’s most reliable medal hope at the Games.
An India-Iran encounter in the men’s final was expected, nay assumed from the moment the draw had been made. The two powerhouses are miles ahead of the rest and any challenge to India’s superiority could only come from the Iranians. The title decider lived up to its billing.
India and Iran traded points early on and were content staying level without getting too adventurous in both attack and defence. Arjun Deshwal and Devank Dalal led India’s raids while captain Sunil Kumar, along with Jaideep and Sumit, held firm in defence.
Amirmohammad Zafar Danesh completed an all-out and the contest remained in balance with Iran taking a one-point lead into half time. Post break, India regrouped: a super tackle and a successful raid by Aslam Inamdar helped India level the score at 20-20.
Iran skipper Fazel Atrachali and Omid Khojasteh Mohammadshah mounted a brief recovery while Ali Samadi tried to earn raiding points. But the turning point came when Arjun set up an all-out that opened up a five-point cushion for India with 10 minutes remaining. Leading 39-32 with under 20 seconds left on the clock, India sealed gold in emphatic fashion.
Earlier, the India women’s team had to fight off a stiff challenge from the 2018 champion for a narrow three-point win. It dominated the first half, at the end of which it led 22-16.
But Iran went on the offensive in the second period, reducing the margin. Pooja and Sanju Devi worked tirelessly, one point at a time, in every raid, as India stayed ahead before retaining the title.

briefs.headline: Men in Blue begin ODI World Cup countdown
briefs.deck: The three-match series against the Windies promises plenty of action; the visiting side will be desperate for a good show in a country where it hasn’t won a bilateral series since 2002
briefs.bodyText:
They were gone. All those thousands of tickets. Gone in a matter of hours. A young cricket fan, who lives near the Greenfield Stadium, still blames himself for not logging in a bit earlier on the day ticket sales opened. He tried the black market, too, though it would have cost him three times the actual price, but no ticket was available.
So much for all those talks about the meaninglessness of bilateral ODI series. The 50-over format has its own charms. Granted, it is no Test match. Nothing is. But it offers an awful lot more than T20 cricket.
The three-match ODI series between India and the West Indies, which begins in Thiruvananthapuram on Sunday (September 26, 2026), indeed promises plenty. With the World Cup just a year away, this is definitely the beginning of the road map for India, though the same cannot be said about the visiting team, which first has to qualify for the game’s showpiece (and this was the team that won the first two editions and lost to India in the final of the third).
Looking ahead — and preparing for — the World Cup is fine. But if you are someone who believes that art is for art’s sake, this is one series you wouldn’t want to miss: you get to watch two of the modern masters, Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma.
This is, of course, the only format they play for India. And they are not going to be around forever. Kohli is 37. Rohit is 39. You hardly would have thought of that when you watched them play in England just a couple of months ago.
This series could also see both reaching more milestones: Kohli needs only 59 more to become the second man to score 15,000 ODI runs after Sachin Tendulkar, while Rohit requires 105 to touch 12,000.
The other top-order batter, skipper Shubman Gill, has been in sublime form and is the world’s No. 1 in the format. He doesn’t have at his disposal the best possible XI because of the ongoing Asian Games and injury concerns, but that opens opportunities for players like Ruturaj Gaikwad, Auqib Nabi and Naman Dhir.
The West Indians will be desperate for a good show in a country where they haven’t won an ODI series since 2002. Shai Hope and his men may not find it easy against the class, experience and skills of India.

briefs.headline: Chess Olympiad: Indian women hold China; men romp to a win
briefs.bodyText:
For the second time inside three days, B. Savitha Shri proved India’s savior. The 19-year-old girl from Chennai ensured India at least got a match point in the penultimate round of the Chess Olympiad at Samarkand on Saturday.
India was trailing 1-2 against the sole leader China, but Savitha’s win on the fourth board over Zhai Mo helped her team draw 2-2, keeping alive the hopes of a medal going into Sunday’s final round. Koneru Humpy and Divya Deshmukh had drawn their games, and Vantika Agrawal lost, and that meant Savitha was in a must-win situation.
This was her eighth win from nine games; she has drawn one and lost none. Thanks in no small measure to the debutant’s superb show, India is in joint second in the women’s event with position with 16 points. China has 18 points and Kazakhstan 17.
In the open section, India is in the sole second position with 17 points, one behind the leader Uzbekistan. Germany, Ukraine and Hungary have 16 points each, setting up an exciting finish.
The Indian men posted a thumping 3.5-0.5 win against the host’s second team, Uzbekistan (2). R. Praggnanandhaa, Nihal Sarin and D. Gukesh scored wins, while Arjun Erigaisi drew.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: Sawan clinches marathon silver; Tajinderpal settles for second spot; Prachi pulls off a surprise
briefs.deck: Questions around selections and accountability of absentee athletes overshadow the impressive performances of the Indians
briefs.bodyText:
A day that began with the longest competitive distance in athletics, producing one of the most precious medals for India, ended with questions around selections and accountability of absentee athletes that overshadowed the impressive performances of those who did turn up to do their best.
Saturday morning at the Asian Games here saw Sawan Barwal, a man who started running marathons only a year ago, break not only his own National record by an incredible 21 seconds (2:11:37s) but also win India’s first Games silver in the event in 44 years. He had already shattered one of the longest standing records in Indian athletics, Shivnath Singh’s 1978 timing of 2:12:00 by running 2:11:58 in April. More importantly, this is only the fourth Indian medal in the Asian marathon and the first outside India.
It had not been easy for the long-distance runner to switch to road races, but Sawan clearly knew what he was capable of. Staying steady with the leader pack but not going too aggressive, he stayed within striking distance and, for a while, looked like the 28-year-old could go all the way before Japan’s Ichitaka Yamashita (2:10:49) edged ahead in the home stretch.
In the evening, Tajinderpal Singh Toor failed to complete his hat-trick of Asian Games gold, settling for silver at the Paloma Mizuho athletics stadium here on Saturday (September 26, 2026) in incessant rain and cold weather that tested every athlete both on the track and field.
Tajinderpal managed the best throw of 20.64 m with a huge effort on his fifth attempt but could not get past Iran Mohammadreza Tayebise, who set a new Games record of 20.81 m, for the top spot. Saudi Arabia’s Mohammed Tolu, who briefly jumped into second place, finished third (20.48). Karanveer Singh finished a disappointing 10th with 18.40.
Prachi Choudhary was a surprise bronze medallist in women’s 400m (53.21s), but the rest were disappointed.
Karthik Unnikrishnan was sixth in the triple jump (16.02 m), while Kiran Pahal was fifth in the 400 m (53.41 s). Vishal T.K. was placed fifth among the men’s 400m (45.48s), and Parul Chaudhary, despite a personal best of 4:09.46, could only manage fourth in women’s 1500m.
Tejaswin Shankar, meanwhile, was leading the decathlon charts with 4,338 points after five events.
But eyebrows were raised when Jyothi Yarraji, silver medallist in the 100m hurdles last time around, and National record holder triple jumper Praveen Chithravel both pulled out of the competition. The two, along with high jumper Sarvesh Kushare, had submitted medical certificates assuring complete fitness before being cleared at the last minute.

briefs.headline: Playing India in their backyard is a challenge, need to grasp and embrace it: West Indies skipper Hope
briefs.deck: “We see great sparks in different series and from different people,” says captain Shai
briefs.bodyText:
West Indies cricket isn’t exactly going through a great time. It hasn’t, for a long time. But ahead of the ODI series against India, starting here on Sunday (September 26, 2026), the captain expressed hope, and not just because of his name.
Captain Shai Hope has expectations of some of the new players and takes heart from individual performances, too. “We see great sparks in different series and from different people,” he said. “It is about repeating that, trying to get those performances for a longer duration, rather than one or two games. We have to try to extend that for two, three, four series. Consistency is the biggest thing for us.”
He sees a lot of potential in the young spinner Vitel Lawes. “I expect him to grow as a left-arm spinner for us,” the captain said.
Hope is excited to play in India. “Playing India in their backyard, always a challenge, which we definitely need to grasp and embrace,” he said.”
